problem: Earlier learned route-instruction followers either used simple worlds with no objects or attributes (Matuszek et al. 2010, laser maps), very restricted output languages (Shimizu & Haas 2009, only 15 labels), or were given object names and predefined spatial terms (Vogel & Jurafsky 2010; Kollar et al. 2010). The strong system for the MacMahon et al. (2006) corpus, MARCO, is fully hand-engineered. No system learned a compositional semantic parser for complex, landmark-rich navigation instructions using only observations of humans following them.
motivation: Understanding free-form route instructions is essential for agents that interact with humans. Annotating instructions with formal meaning representations is expensive, whereas recordings of people following instructions are cheap. The key observation is that an instruction corresponds to an unobserved plan, not directly to the observed action sequence, and different people describe the same route very differently (landmarks vs. step counts, 'coat rack' vs. 'hatrack'). So the latent plan must be inferred before a parser can be trained.
key_idea: Infer a latent formal navigation plan for each instruction from the observed follower actions and world state (a landmark-annotated plan), prune it with a cross-situationally learned word-to-subgraph lexicon, and use the resulting (instruction, plan) pairs to train a supervised semantic parser (KRISP) whose outputs are executed by MARCO.
insight: Training-data precision matters more than recall for the parser. Landmarks plans have high recall (85.46) but low precision (45.42), and the KRISP parser trained on them collapses: parse F1 38.39 (Table 3) and 2.66% complete-instruction success (Table 4). Lexicon-based refinement keeps both the precision of basic plans and the recall of landmarks plans (inferred-plan F1 78.32 vs 66.27 basic, Table 2), which gives the best learned parser (F1 68.37). Modeling landmarks only pays off on long multi-sentence instructions: basic plans are slightly better on single sentences (56.99 vs 54.40), but refined landmarks plans win on complete paragraphs (16.18 vs 13.99) because verification landmarks let the executor recover from small errors.
method: Basic plan construction: converts the observed follower action sequence into a formal plan containing only Turn(left/right) and Travel(steps) actions.

Landmarks plan construction: simulates the actions in the world and interleaves Verify steps listing all landmarks (floor patterns, wall paintings, furniture) observed after each action; high recall but many extraneous details.

Lexicon learning (Algorithm 1): for each unigram/bigram w, collects the graph plans of instructions containing w and repeatedly adds pairwise graph intersections (greedy largest-common-subgraph removal) until convergence. Candidates are scored by Score(w,g)=p(g|w)-p(g|¬w), keeping the top k=1000 and adding entries with score above t=0.4 to the lexicon.

Plan refinement: repeatedly picks the highest-scoring lexical entry (w,g) with w in the instruction and g in the plan, removes w and marks occurrences of g. Unmarked nodes are then pruned, giving a refined plan that conservatively keeps only content referenced by words.

Semantic parser learning: KRISP (SVM classifiers with string kernels over CFG productions, chosen for robustness to noisy supervision) is trained on the (sentence, refined plan) pairs to map new instructions to plans such as Turn(), Verify(front: SOFA).

Execution: parsed plans are converted into MARCO compound action specifications and run by MARCO's executor. The executor interleaves perception and action and has error-recovery and implicit-command inference; it is non-deterministic when plans are underspecified, so each plan is run 10 times.

setting.backbone: KRISP semantic parser (SVM + string kernels, trained from scratch) + hand-engineered MARCO execution module
setting.training_data: MacMahon et al. (2006) route-instruction corpus (SAIL): 706 instructions from 6 instructors over 126 start/goal pairs in 3 virtual worlds, with 1-15 human followers each. It is manually segmented into 3236 single-sentence instruction/action pairs (actions aligned by majority of followers plus map knowledge; ~300 unmatched sentences discarded). Training uses 2 maps, and the lexicon is also learned from them. No prior linguistic knowledge is used.
setting.observation: symbolic world-state description (floor patterns, wall paintings, furniture at intersections) perceived through the MARCO simulated environment
setting.action_space: discrete: turn left, turn right, move forward from one intersection to the next
setting.simulator: MARCO virtual indoor hallway environments (MacMahon et al. 2006; 3 maps)
setting.privileged: symbolic landmark/object perception from the simulated world (no raw vision); training instructions were manually segmented into sentences and aligned to actions

numbers_note: There is no official split: evaluation is leave-one-map-out cross-validation over the 3 maps (test map unseen), averaged across folds. I mapped this to 'test-unseen'. Parse precision/recall/F1 (partial correctness vs. human-annotated plans, Table 3) are attached to the single-sentence entries. Table 2 also reports inferred-training-plan quality (Refined landmarks P/R/F1 78.54/78.10/78.32; Basic 81.46/55.88/66.27; Landmarks 45.42/85.46/59.29). Baselines in Table 4, not own methods: simple generative model 11.08/2.15, MARCO 77.87/55.69, human followers N/A/69.64.
results: On complete multi-sentence instructions, the system trained on lexicon-refined landmarks plans reaches the exact destination in 16.18% of trials. This beats basic plans (13.99), unrefined landmarks plans (2.66) and a language-agnostic generative baseline (2.15), but remains below a parser trained on human-annotated plans (26.15), the hand-engineered MARCO (55.69) and human followers (69.64). On single sentences, the learned systems (basic 56.99, refined 54.40) approach the human-annotated-plan upper bound (58.29). Plan refinement raises inferred-plan F1 to 78.32 and parser F1 to 68.37.
limitations: The pipeline is sequential with no feedback loops, so errors in plan inference propagate to parser learning; execution success is not used as a learning signal.

Absolute performance on full paragraph instructions is low (16.18% vs 55.69% for hand-engineered MARCO). The method relies on manual segmentation of instructions and sentence-to-action alignment, symbolic landmark perception, and MARCO's hand-built executor.
It is evaluated only in three small discrete simulated hallway worlds, with a symbolic formal plan language; there is no raw perception or real robot.
